Insightful paper on recursive self-improvement with a frozen LLM. (bookmark it) Memento 3 clears every level of all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games and uses 44% of the human action count. The underlying LLM is never updated. How it works: The agent writes what it believes about the environment as a natural-language rulebook, then compiles that rulebook into code that predicts the next state. A new version is kept only if replaying the code reproduces every transition the agent has observed, cell for cell. In an Atari Pong case study, the learned model drives a controller that wins 21 to 0 in three games without further LLM calls. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11794 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/memento-3-model-based-recursive-self-improvement-through-reflective-rulebooks-2610.11794

Interesting new research from Meta Superintelligence Labs It discusses how reward hacking affects coordination in multi-agent coding systems. Coding agents on a team share code, memory, and plans, so a reward hack one agent learns gets passed to the others. The paper traces this through three channels. Hacks move through shared code, through shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Agents on small open-weight models can induce hacking in stronger closed-weight agents. On hard tasks, the hacking can grow along a chain even after the original agent has left, because the code collects more convincing justifications on the way. It also biases task routing toward the hacking agents and survives candidate aggregation. So how do you mitigate this problem? The authors suggest that code review by the coder or by a separate verifier reduces the hacks that get delivered. If your agents share a repo, the review step is the first thing to add. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12822 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/reward-hacking-as-a-transmissible-strategy-in-multi-agent-coding-systems-2610.12822

Own your intelligence stack, folks! If you train or fine-tune your own models, you also need a way to prove they are yours once the weights are out in the world. Model fingerprinting does this. The Fingerprinting Leaderboard from @Sentient_found is an open benchmark for these methods. It scores each one on how much model quality it keeps, how well it survives removal attempts, and how reliably the owner can detect it. Models cost millions to train and minutes to copy. Fine-tuning and distillation can erase where they came from.
